title: “I Am Joseph”: The Brothers Reconciled
summary: Overcome by Judah's plea, Joseph sends his attendants out and reveals himself to his brothers, weeping so loudly that the Egyptians hear. He tells them that although they sold him, God sent him ahead to preserve their lives, and he invites the whole family to settle in Goshen. Pharaoh confirms the invitation, the brothers return with wagons and gifts, and Jacob, stunned at first, revives and resolves to go and see his son.
story: This is the climax of the Joseph story. The dreams, the pit, the prison, and the tests of Genesis 42 to 44 all lead to this room, where Joseph can no longer keep up the mask. His first question is about his father, and his first explanation is about God. What the brothers meant as the end of Joseph, God used to put him in the one place from which he could save them. The chapter also moves the larger story of Genesis forward. The family of promise, seventy people in all, is about to leave Canaan for Egypt, where it will grow into a nation and eventually become enslaved, setting the stage for the book of Exodus. Jacob's final words here, “I will go to see him before I die”, launch the move that Genesis 46 will describe.
historical:
Joseph says the famine has lasted two years, with five more to come, years in which there will be neither plowing nor harvest (v. 6). In Egypt that meant a Nile flood too low to water the fields. He calls himself a father to Pharaoh, lord of his household, and ruler over Egypt (v. 8). The first of these titles may reflect the Egyptian title god's father, held by certain priests and senior officials, though the Hebrew phrase is also natural as a description of a trusted counselor. Pharaoh's generous welcome (vv. 16-20) reflects Joseph's standing at court; Pharaoh offers the best of the land and carts from Egypt to carry the women and children.

Goshen, where Joseph plans to settle the family, was in the eastern Nile Delta, though its exact boundaries are uncertain. Joseph says they will be near him, which suggests that the royal court or Joseph's residence was not far from the Delta. The three hundred shekels of silver given to Benjamin amount to roughly three and a half kilograms, since a shekel was a weight of about eleven or twelve grams, not a coin.
cultural:
Joseph's weeping is not a private sob. He wept so loudly that the Egyptians outside heard, a public breaking of the reserve expected of an official. Embracing, weeping on the neck, and kissing were the signs of family reunion in the ancient Near East, as when Esau embraced Jacob (33:4). Gifts of clothing were gifts of honor, and the story has been marked by garments throughout: the robe the brothers stripped from Joseph, and now new garments for each of them. Benjamin again receives more, five sets of clothes and silver, the same kind of singling out that once provoked envy.

Joseph's parting instruction (v. 24) is usually translated “Do not quarrel on the way!” The Hebrew verb can mean to be agitated, whether by anger or by fear, so some translators take it as a warning against blaming one another for the past, and others as a reassurance not to be afraid on the road. Both suit the moment.
literary: The revelation is told in short, charged speech. “I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?” is followed by the brothers' stunned silence, then a second, fuller self-identification: “I am Joseph, your brother,” and then, “the one you sold into Egypt!” Joseph does not pretend the sale did not happen. Then comes the theological heart of the Joseph story. Three times Joseph says that God sent him (vv. 5, 7, 8), and the climax is the reversal of agents in verse 8: “it was not you who sent me here, but God.” The verb sell (vv. 4, 5) is answered by the verb send. The chapter then shifts to logistics: the message to Jacob, Pharaoh's invitation, wagons, provisions. It closes in Canaan with Jacob's disbelief and revival, and the narrator calls him Israel as he makes his decision (v. 28), the name God gave him as the bearer of the promise.

outline.t: Joseph makes himself known to his brothers
Joseph's message to Jacob and the brothers' embrace
Pharaoh's invitation and the gifts for the family
Jacob hears the news and is revived

doctrines.note: Joseph's words in verses 5 to 8 are among the Bible's clearest statements of providence. God did not merely repair what the brothers broke; he was at work through the whole chain of events to save life. The brothers remain responsible for selling Joseph, and God remains sovereign over what came of it.

Joseph says God sent him to preserve a remnant and to save lives by a great deliverance (v. 7). The vocabulary of remnant and deliverance, here used of survival through famine, will become the language of God's rescue of his people through judgment and exile.

Reconciliation in this chapter includes truth-telling (“the one you sold into Egypt”), release from guilt (“do not be distressed”), and practical provision for the whole household. Forgiveness is not left as a feeling; Joseph gives land, food, and a future.

words.note: Shalach, to send. The key verb of Joseph's speech: God sent me before you (vv. 5, 7), and it was not you who sent me here, but God (v. 8). The brothers sold; God sent. The same verb is used for the sending of prophets and messengers, and here it turns a crime into a commission without erasing the crime.

She'erit, remnant, what is left over after loss. Joseph says God sent him to preserve them as a remnant on the earth (v. 7). The word becomes important in the prophets, who speak of a remnant that survives judgment and carries God's promise forward (for example Isaiah 10:20-22). Here the whole family of promise is that remnant.

Michyah, preservation of life, from the verb to live. Joseph says it was to save lives, literally for preservation of life, that God sent him ahead (v. 5). The purpose of everything he endured is expressed in a single word: life.

christ: Joseph's claim that God sent him through his brothers' crime is the Old Testament's clearest parallel to how the apostles spoke about the cross. At Pentecost Peter told the crowd that Jesus was handed over by God's set plan and foreknowledge, and that they had put him to death by lawless hands (Acts 2:23). God's purpose and human guilt stand together in both stories without either cancelling the other. Stephen notes that Joseph made himself known to his brothers on their second visit (Acts 7:13), and Christians have seen in the scene a picture of the risen Christ making himself known to those who abandoned him and sending them out with good news. The link is thematic, but the shape is the same: the rejected brother becomes the one who saves, and he greets his betrayers with tears and provision rather than revenge.

hard.q: If God sent Joseph to Egypt, are the brothers excused for selling him?
hard.a:
Joseph does not excuse them. He names their act plainly, “the one you sold into Egypt,” before he says anything about God. What he refuses to do is let their guilt be the last word. The Bible holds together two claims that can seem to compete: human beings are fully responsible for the evil they choose, and God is sovereign over the outcome, even of evil acts. Genesis 50:20 states the same point with two intentions at work in one event.

Christians explain the relationship differently. The Reformed tradition speaks of God ordaining all that comes to pass, including evil acts, without being the author of sin or removing human responsibility. Other traditions, including Arminian and many Catholic and Orthodox theologians, prefer to say that God permits evil acts he does not will and then overrules them for good. Both agree on what this chapter teaches: the brothers did wrong, God was not the author of their envy, and God's purpose to save was not defeated by it. Joseph's words are also a pastoral act. He speaks them to men terrified of his revenge, not as a general excuse for sin.

questions: Joseph names what his brothers did and in the same breath tells them not to be distressed. How can forgiveness tell the truth about a wrong and still release the person who did it?
Joseph says, “it was not you who sent me here, but God.” What might change if you looked at a past injury through that lens, and what are the dangers of doing so too quickly?
Jacob could not believe the news until he saw the wagons. What has helped you believe good news from God when it seemed too good to be true?
